title: Reduction of anxiety, depression and decisional conflict among patients' relatives through Advance Care Planning (ACP) prior to major oncological surgery – a prospective, single-centre, controlled interventional study with a sequential prospective control group
summary:
Background
Before major cancer surgery, patients and their relatives are often under considerable stress. If complications occur after the operation, patients may no longer be able to make decisions for themselves. Relatives then have to help decide on further treatment, often without knowing what the patient would have wanted. This can cause anxiety, depression and great uncertainty when making decisions. In what is known as advance care planning, patients talk early on with professionals and their relatives about their wishes in case they can no longer decide for themselves. These wishes are then put in writing.

Research question
We want to find out whether offering advance care planning before major cancer surgery can reduce anxiety, depression and uncertainty in decision-making among relatives.

Methods
Patients at University Hospital Augsburg who are scheduled for major cancer surgery take part in the study together with a person close to them. First, a comparison group is enrolled that receives usual care. The surgeons are then specifically trained to hold advance care planning conversations. After that, a second group is enrolled. This group receives a specially developed decision aid in advance. Building on this, the surgeons hold a conversation with the patient and their relative together during the information discussion before the operation. This conversation is about the patient’s wishes in case they can no longer make decisions for themselves. At the start of the study, three days after the operation, and one, three, six and twelve months later, relatives complete short questionnaires about anxiety, depression and uncertainty in decision-making. We also record how often a trusted person is given written authority to make health decisions, and how long patients stay in hospital after the operation. Finally, we compare the results of both groups.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Designation of a primary contact person (the relative does not necessarily have to hold a health care power of attorney or be a family member)
The relative is present at the preoperative surgical informed consent discussion
Written informed consent from both the patient and the relative
Exclusion criteria:
Refusal to participate in the study
Lack of capacity to consent
The patient is under legal guardianship
Language barrier
